outline: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA)
mechanism: In ALCAPA, the left coronary artery originates from the pulmonary artery rather than the aorta. Early after birth, relatively high pulmonary artery pressure can maintain some antegrade perfusion through the anomalous vessel. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall, left-coronary perfusion pressure decreases and flow can reverse toward the low-pressure pulmonary artery; collateral flow from the right coronary system is then partly lost into the pulmonary artery (coronary steal), producing left-ventricular myocardial ischemia.
vignette: A 6-week-old infant is evaluated for recurrent episodes of intense crying, pallor, diaphoresis, and tachypnea during feeding. The infant was well during the first days after birth. Echocardiography shows left ventricular systolic dysfunction and mitral regurgitation. The left coronary artery arises from the main pulmonary artery rather than the aortic root.
lead: Which of the following mechanisms most directly explains the onset of this infant's myocardial ischemia during the transition to postnatal circulation?
correct: A fall in pulmonary vascular resistance lowers pulmonary artery pressure, promoting reduced antegrade and then retrograde flow through the anomalous left coronary artery into the pulmonary artery
distractors: Rising aortic pressure produces flow limitation in an acute-angle intramural left coronary artery arising from the opposite aortic sinus
Feeding-related tachycardia produces ischemia by systolic compression of an intramyocardial left coronary segment
Antegrade flow through a coronary-to-pulmonary arterial fistula bypasses the myocardial capillary bed and produces a steal phenomenon
The postnatal rise in systemic vascular resistance raises left ventricular oxygen demand while antegrade pulmonary-artery-to-left-coronary flow remains preserved
distractor_notes: Acute-angle ostial narrowing and an intramural/interarterial course can make a coronary artery arising from the opposite aortic sinus hemodynamically significant. This infant's left coronary artery instead originates from the pulmonary artery; the relevant postnatal mechanism is falling pulmonary arterial pressure with loss and reversal of left-coronary perfusion, not an aortic intramural course.

An intramyocardial coronary course (myocardial bridge) can rarely cause ischemia through systolic vessel compression. No intramyocardial course is described here, and that mechanism does not explain why ALCAPA becomes symptomatic as pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall after birth.

A coronary artery fistula can cause steal by maintaining antegrade flow that bypasses the myocardial capillary bed into a low-resistance chamber or vessel. ALCAPA is mechanistically different: the anomalous left coronary originates from the pulmonary artery, and after pulmonary pressure falls, flow tends to reverse from the higher-pressure coronary collateral network into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery.

Systemic vascular resistance does rise after placental separation and can increase left ventricular afterload, making this a plausible supply-demand alternative. However, ALCAPA does not preserve stable antegrade pulmonary-artery-to-left-coronary perfusion; the critical change is the fall in pulmonary pressure/resistance, which reduces antegrade flow and promotes retrograde coronary steal.
key_expl: The infant has ALCAPA. Soon after birth, pulmonary artery pressure remains relatively high, so the anomalous left coronary artery can still receive some antegrade flow. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall, left-coronary perfusion pressure falls and antegrade flow diminishes. Blood supplied through right-to-left coronary collaterals can then run retrograde through the anomalous left coronary artery into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery, creating coronary steal and causing left-ventricular ischemia, dysfunction, and secondary mitral regurgitation.
objective: Explain why infants with ALCAPA often become symptomatic after an initially well neonatal period: falling pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure reduce antegrade left-coronary perfusion and promote retrograde coronary steal into the pulmonary artery.
clues: feeding-associated crying, pallor, diaphoresis, and tachypnea
left coronary artery arises from the main pulmonary artery
